newsitem.title: GERMANY: German debt futures seek to extend record gains.
newsitem.headline: German debt futures seek to extend record gains.

text.p: German Bunds and futures will seek to extend the record gains posted on Tuesday after the DTB March Bund futures contract reached a new all-time record high at 103.00 and maintained the gains, traders said.
At 1325 GMT, DTB March Bund futures were up 33 basis points at 102.98 shortly after breaking strong resistance at 102.99 to trade at 103.00 before paring some gains.
The benchmark 10-year benchmark cash Bund due January 2007 was at 103.17 for a yield of 5.57 percent, up from Monday's closing level at 102.88.
The record gains came in moderate dealings, with many players away on Tuesday for regional pre-Lent holidays.

"The volumes have been very thin and a lot of people are not paying attention to the market," said one Frankfurt trader. "It will be a question as to whether we can sustain these levels on Wednesday when the market is back at full-strength."
The market's gains came mainly from technical factors after March futures broke a series of support levels between 102.60 and 102.99, groping its way higher throughout the session.
Few fresh market fundamentals were available to influence dealings as the focus remained on spreads against the U.S.
Traders shrugged off a real one percent drop in German wholesale turnover in 1996 compared with 1995.

But the influence of economic data, and any interest rate fantasies the market may have for a Bundesbank repo rate cut, will be influenced by the release on Wednesday or Thursday of German retail sales data and Thursday's U.S. jobless claims.
A number of factors have supported the run-up to the record level, including ongoing worries about persistently high German unemployment and few worries about inflation.
But some traders said the market may be due for a consolidation before advancing into unknown territory.

Another looming factor is this week's quarterly treasury refunding in the U.S. amid concerns that a poor performance in one of the auctions could spark a sell-off in Germany due to the market's reliance on the U.S. for direction.
"These have been some heady profits and one has to start wondering how long these can keep going," said one trader. "A lot will still depend on how U.S. prices keep moving."
